previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, a history of kidney transplant, and multiple comorbidities was admitted due to a new vesicular rash concerning for varicella infection. She had recent exposure to her father with shingles and no prior vaccination or immunity. Diagnosis was confirmed by positive varicella direct antigen test. She was treated with seven days of IV acyclovir and IV fluids to protect her renal function, with stable creatinine throughout. The rash progressed to crusting with no new lesions, and she was no longer infectious at discharge. Immunosuppressive therapy was adjusted temporarily, with Cellcept halved and later restored. Glycemic control improved with ongoing insulin pump management. She remained afebrile with no complications such as pneumonia or encephalitis. She was discharged home on her baseline medications with follow-up planned for liver and kidney function.

Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted because you have had constipation for several 
days and have felt weak. An abdominal x-ray did not show an 
acute obstruction. We also performed a CT scan of your abdomen 
which also did not show any obstruction to cause your 
constipation. Since you did not find relief after giving you 
appropriate medications to relieve constipation, we consulted 
Gastroentrology. They felt that your constipation was due to 
inactivity from being in the hospital for several days. Also, 
the codeine you received may have exacerbated your condition. To 
ensure your bowels were moving appropriately, a gastric emptying 
study was performed. It showed you had delayed emptying.  At 
4hrs, there were 30% of residue in your stomach.  No other 
abnormalities were noted. 

 We continued to give you medication for constipation. Your 
bowels moved some as you did pass gas. You also intermittently 
were able to tolerate food. We felt you were stable to leave the 
hospital. We will prescribe you medication to take for your 
bowels. You should make sure you drink plenty of fluids to 
maintain hydration.  Please follow up with you GI doctor. 

Your new medications include:
Senna 1 tab by mouth daily
Miralax 17 grams by mouth daily
Dulcolax 100 mg by mouth twice a day
Reglan 10 mg by mouth four times a day
Protonix 40 mg daily
Cytotec 200 mcg twice a day

You should contact your doctor or go directly to the emergency 
room if you experience severe abdominal pain, inability to pass 
gas, severe constipation, fevers, inability to tolerate food or 
any other symptom that is concerning to you.

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  No bowel movement x5 days.

COMPARISON:  Comparison is made to CT from ___.

FINDINGS:  Two frontal radiographs of the abdomen were included one aligned in
the upright and the other in supine position.  Upright radiograph reveals
several air-fluid levels throughout the lower abdomen bilaterally.  A moderate
amount of gas is seen throughout the colon, with no definite evidence of
colonic distention.  There is no small bowel dilation.  There is no
pneumatosis or free gas.  Scattered atherosclerotic calcifications are
visualized throughout the abdomen.  Included osseous structures are
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:  Scattered air-fluid levels without evidence of high grade
obstruction.  Mild ileus or early obstruction not excluded.

INDICATION:  ___ woman with constipation.

COMPARISON:  Supine and erect abdominal radiograph from ___.

FINDINGS:

Air-fluid levels are seen on the upright radiograph.  No large or small bowel
dilatation is seen and air is seen throughout the large and small bowel.
Atherosclerotic calcifications are seen throughout the abdomen.

The visualized osseous structures are unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:

Multiple small air-fluid levels with no dilated loops of bowel. Unchanged from
prior.

EXAM:  CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast, ___.

INDICATION:  Constipation, and recent abnormal KUBs.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiographs from ___ and ___, and multiple
previous studies.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric CT of the abdomen and pelvis with oral and intravenous
contrast.

CT ABDOMEN:  Visualized lung bases are clear, except for mild linear
atelectasis at the left lung base.

Liver contour is normal.  There is subtle hypodensity in the left lobe of the
liver adjacent to the falciform ligament, most probably representing an area
of focal fatty infiltration.  No other liver lesions are seen.  There is no
biliary ductal dilatation or ascites.  Gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, and
adrenal glands are unremarkable.  Stomach and intra-abdominal loops of bowel
are normal.  There is no obstruction.  There is no free air, free fluid, or
abnormal intra-abdominal lymph nodes.  Native kidneys are atrophic, with
multiple vascular calcifications.  There is slight enhancement of the native
kidneys, but no excretion of contrast.

CT PELVIS:  Transplant kidney in the left lower quadrant enhances and excretes
contrast normally.  There is no perinephric inflammatory change or fluid
collection.  There is no hydronephrosis.  Previous right lower quadrant renal
transplant, slightly enhances, but does not excrete contrast.  Pelvic loops of
large and small bowel are unremarkable.  There is a small amount of free
pelvic fluid, likely physiologic.  Urinary bladder and adnexa are
unremarkable.  There is no abnormal pelvic or inguinal lymph node.

There are no osseous lesions suspicious for malignancy.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of bowel obstruction.  No acute findings in the
abdomen/pelvis.
